R_H1.passageTitle: A Weekly Event with Room for Walkers

passages.label: A
passages.text: At parkrun, people can be active without buying a ticket or travelling at a competitive speed. Volunteers organise the free five-kilometre Saturday events, and a participant can register once and bring a barcode to record a time. The result shows what happened on the course, and it gives no number for calories used, but seeing progress in regular exercise can help a person build self-esteem.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The organisation makes walking part of the event. There is no time limit, and a volunteer called the Tail Walker stays behind the other participants and finishes last. The role helps account for everyone on the course. This changes what finishing slowly means: the event has planned for it, rather than treating it as failure. It is useful to recognise that participation includes several speeds. Someone can be active without needing to beat other people or match the pace of an experienced runner.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Other volunteers support the event. Course checks, directing participants, keeping time and scanning barcodes are different jobs. Course safety is a serious responsibility, but helping is also a form of participation. The organisation's volunteering strategy gives helping the same respect as walking or running. It describes social connections, skills and a sense of belonging among the benefits of volunteering. Those aims help explain why the event is more than a list of finishing times.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Junior parkrun has a different format. Its Sunday events cover two kilometres and are for children aged four to fourteen. Volunteers are placed so that children remain within sight of a marshal. Children under eleven usually need an adult to bring them, remain at the event and collect them at the finish. Adults can accompany children on the course, but the children's results list has its own age rules. The shorter distance therefore comes with a separate organisation, rather than simply copying every rule of the longer event. Some families pack water or a snack before they set off, when it can be useful to think about what the children will enjoy eating later rather than buying junk food on the way.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A weekly event can support a healthy lifestyle by offering a regular time for physical activity. A balanced diet is another part of daily life. A portion of food after a walk has its own nutritional value, but finishing the event does not make food choices for a person. The CDC describes moderate activity as generally safe for most adults. People who suffer from conditions including heart disease can ask a doctor about suitable kinds and amounts of activity. It is worth learning to recognise the difference between being welcome on a course and knowing what level of effort is suitable.

passages.label: F
passages.text: A registration system lets walkers sign up for an event and join in without having to try out for a competition. Someone may take up walking as a personal habit, while a social commitment offers opportunities to relax or manage stress. The opportunity to participate regularly can matter more than improvement in recorded performance.

R_H2.passageTitle: How Hard Is an Exercise Session?

passages.label: A
passages.text: What makes a walk count as exercise? The CDC uses intensity to mean how hard a person’s body works during physical activity. Moving changes breathing and heart rate, but the same walk can feel easy for one person and difficult for another. The signs of a serious health problem call for a different decision. A person who has been active for years may find a hill easier than someone recovering from a serious illness. The name of an activity alone cannot tell us how hard an individual worked.

passages.label: B
passages.text: One approach compares effort with a person's own fitness. On the CDC's scale of relative intensity, zero means the effort needed to sit, whereas ten represents the greatest effort possible. Five or six indicates moderate activity, and vigorous activity starts at seven or eight. The activity that feels vigorous to someone of average fitness can feel moderate to a very fit person, because the scale describes effort for that individual rather than age or sporting skill.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The talk test offers another way to recognise the difference. During moderate exercise, a person can usually talk but cannot sing. During vigorous exercise, speaking more than a few words requires a pause for breath. This comparison does not require a watch. It connects a technical idea with an ordinary action. The CDC lists brisk walking and doubles tennis among moderate activities, while jogging and singles tennis appear among vigorous ones. Being active does not always mean working at the highest intensity.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A second approach looks at the energy used during movement without considering someone's fitness. This is absolute intensity. Its unit compares an activity with sitting quietly. As work becomes harder, the amount of energy used increases. Calories also measure energy, but the two measures answer different questions. The CDC links to a separate table of energy used in common activities. A person's breathing and a table's estimate should not be treated as identical information about an exercise session. Knowing how much energy an exercise session uses cannot tell a person how often junk food appears in the meals they eat.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Time matters as well as effort. The CDC describes 150 minutes of moderate activity each week as a target for adults, along with muscle-strengthening work on two days. An activity diary can record minutes of regular exercise, while a food diary may record the calories and nutritional content in a portion. These records describe different parts of a healthy lifestyle. A balanced diet is not a measure of exercise intensity. People who suffer from conditions such as heart disease can ask a health professional which activities are suitable.

passages.label: F
passages.text: An activity diary can show how one personal habit changes. People who work out to stay in shape might track physical effort. They can take up walking, reduce their speed when they get tired and still build performance. A person returning after an illness may value a routine that helps them relax.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Who should take responsibility for reducing sugar intake? One British policy changed the question from what families buy to what companies put in their drinks, and the Soft Drinks Industry Levy began on 6 April 2018. It was meant to encourage producers to change recipes and help address childhood obesity, and a levy is a tax, but this one operated through the production and import of qualifying drinks. Its design aimed to influence the products available, rather than simply telling each customer to make a different choice.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Under the original design, the amount of sugar set the rate. A qualifying drink containing at least five but less than eight grams of sugar in 100 millilitres attracted the lower rate. Drinks at or above eight grams attracted the higher rate. These figures show what the rules were when the levy started. The government could change the rules later. The launch announcement said that more than half of manufacturers had already reduced sugar before the levy began. Changing a recipe could therefore alter a company's payment as well as what was in the drink.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The government reported a 46 per cent fall in the average sugar content of drinks within the levy from 2015 to 2020, with greater weight given to drinks with high sales. An educational message can ask families to cut down on sugar or change an unhealthy habit. An individual may give up one drink due to a personal or social influence, but sales figures do not prove any change in physical activity or mental well-being. They provide one measure of whether the levy helped producers reduce sugar content.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Information for families developed alongside action directed at industry. In 2014, a Change4Life advertising campaign used television, radio and online adverts to encourage food and drink swaps. A 2018 campaign promoted healthier snacks, and an improved Food Scanner app displayed calories, sugar, salt and saturated fat. This made nutritional information easier to examine. The size of a portion, meaning an amount served, still matters when interpreting a label: information about a small amount does not automatically describe everything in a large bottle. Communication helps explain choices, whereas a tax can influence producers' decisions. An educational programme can add to such public messages by teaching people to compare labels for equal amounts of two drinks.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The levy and the separate campaign address different parts of the problem. A nutritional label helps people recognise the difference between calories in a portion and the total in a bottle. Drinking less sugar is one part of a balanced diet, just as physical activity and regular exercise can be part of a healthy lifestyle. A label does not establish whether children eat less junk food overall. Establishing changes in obesity, heart disease or other serious outcomes would require evidence that covers what people eat, drink and do over time.
